title: Work as practice
hook: a Chan saying tied to Baizhang: a day without work, a day without food

segments.voice: Yesterday: four parts, and your line was the same. Which of the four parts did that budget line turn out to belong to? Day three hundred eighty-one.

An old Chan master, very old by every account, still goes out each day to work in the monastery fields with the younger monks. They worry about him. So one day they hide his tools. He doesn't argue. He just doesn't eat that day. When they ask him why, he answers, so the story goes: a day without work is a day without food. The master is Baizhang, in eighth-century China, and his line became one of the best-known sayings in Zen. Today: work as practice.
screen: `AN OLD MAN IN THE FIELDS.` → `THE TOOLS GO MISSING.` → `A DAY WITHOUT WORK.`

segments.voice: Baizhang's name is tied to something new in Buddhist history. In India, by the old monastic rules, monks didn't farm or dig the soil. They walked for alms and lived on what the village gave. When the teaching traveled to China, things changed. Monasteries were often far from towns, and begging was viewed less kindly there. Chan communities began to farm, cook, haul water and chop wood for themselves. Tradition credits Baizhang with the first rules for Chan monasteries, built around shared labor. The original text of those rules is lost, and historians think much of the story was told later, but the ideal stuck. Work wasn't a break from practice. It was practice. In Japan the same idea carries the name samu: work done as meditation, sweeping, weeding, scrubbing, in silence and fully. That connects to right livelihood in a quiet way. Most of us can't choose every task in a job. We can choose how we're present for it. Sweeping a floor with your whole attention and sweeping it while rehearsing an argument are two different afternoons, even if the floor ends up equally clean. The saying is sometimes taken as a hard rule: no work, no lunch. The story suggests something gentler. Baizhang isn't punishing anyone, not even himself. For him, working and eating simply belonged together, the way breathing in and breathing out do. Leaving one out didn't make sense.
screen: `IN INDIA, MONKS DIDN'T FARM.` · `CHAN MONASTERIES PICK UP HOES.` · `SAMU: WORK AS MEDITATION.` · `TWO AFTERNOONS, ONE CLEAN FLOOR.` · then, large: `WORK IS PRACTICE.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. Choose one task you'll do today anyway: the dishes, an email, folding laundry, a spreadsheet. Picture doing it the Chan way. Not faster, not slower. Fully. Your hands on what they're touching. Your attention on this plate, this sentence, this towel. When the mind runs ahead to the next task, notice it, and come back to this one. Rehearse it here for a while, with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Work as practice. Baizhang's saying, a day without work is a day without food: in Chan, ordinary labor is part of the path.
Your line: work is practice. Today, do one job fully, with nothing else in your head, and notice how it feels when it's done. Day three hundred eighty-one.

howItsDone: In Chan and Zen monasteries, daily work periods are part of the schedule, and residents and retreatants clean, cook and garden in silence as practice; in Japanese temples this is called samu.

fork.setup: you're an elderly Chan master. your students have hidden your tools so you'll rest. what does the story say you do?
options: scold them and find the tools.
fork.reveal: Baizhang skips his meal and explains: a day without work is a day without food. no scolding, just the two belonging together.

original.say: yee RUH boo DZWOH, yee RUH boo SHUR
original.note: Chinese, yī rì bù zuò, yī rì bù shí: a day without work, a day without food, the saying tied to Baizhang Huaihai.

trapdoor: what you thought: no work, no lunch is a strict rule.
what it means: for Baizhang, working and eating, like practice and daily life, belonged together.
what a scholar hears: the 'pure rules' credited to Baizhang survive only in later versions, and since the Indian Vinaya forbade monks to dig the soil, Chan farming was a real shift in monastic life.

sources.ref: Baizhang Huaihai (traditionally 720–814), the saying 'a day without work, a day without food', as recorded in later Chan biographies

notes: The hidden-tools story and saying are recorded in Song-dynasty Chan sources (e.g. lamp records) rather than in contemporary documents; told as 'so the story goes'. Confirm sources.
Baizhang's dates are traditional (720–814; some give 749–814); the script says only 'very old' and 'eighth-century China' (he lived into the ninth).
Historians (e.g. Foulk, Poceski) question how much of the 'Baizhang rules' tradition is his; the script says the original text is lost and much was told later.
'Begging was viewed less kindly there' is a common generalization about Chinese attitudes; Keeper may want to soften or remove.
